newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-NZ Treasurer Peters bullish on economy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-NZ Treasurer Peters bullish on economy.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters on Friday welcomed recent falls in interest rates and said he expected a restoration of business confidence.

In an interview with Reuters in his home electorate of Tauranga, Peters said recent surveys showing a decline in business confidence in New Zealand had been carried out when significant information, such as March quarter inflation data, was not known to the market.
"I think it is all relative. I think there will be a restoration of confidence. It is clear the economy has troughed some time ago and things are beginning to pick up," Peters said.
He said New Zealand deserved a triple A rating from the ratings agencies.
"We are deserving of one. When the two institutions Standard and Poor's and Moody's come visiting, which is pretty soon, we have got some good news to tell them," he said.

"I expect their assessment to reflect the reality of an economy which is being soundly managed with healthy surpluses, a slightly slower debt repayment schedule, and nevertheless with areas of critical social expenditure that can't be ignored (which are) being addressed," Peters said. He added another factor was the removal of "the instability factor of politics".
Peters said the date of the budget had not yet been set concretely but would be in mid to late June.
Asked how the markets would react to the budget, he said, "I think they will react positively because we are getting the message over.

"The days of dramatic budget surprises are over. The March 4 budget policy statement clearly set out where we intend to go, now it is a matter of the detail. There will be some good news for a lot of people."
Peters said the planned September referendum on compulsory superannuation was not causing uncertainties for long term budget forecasting, as some commentators fear.

"The numbers are robust whether the referendum is yes or no," he said. The referendum may herald the introduction of a new, government-regulated but privately-managed pension savings scheme which has been dubbed 'compulsory super'.
Peters reiterated that he believed the speed of the rise in the New Zealand dollar had been arrested.
"That dollar rose 26 percent in the three years to December (1996). If anyone is concerned about exporters they will (welcome) that the velocity of it has been arrested."
